difference: A queue holds work until a consumer pulls it; fan-out pushes one message to many subscribers; an event bus routes matching events to targets.

sides.label: Amazon SNS
sides.pickWhen: One message must reach several subscribers.

sides.label: Amazon EventBridge
sides.pickWhen: A rule should invoke targets when a matching event occurs.

difference: KMS is a managed key service integrated with AWS encryption; CloudHSM is dedicated hardware security modules the customer controls.

sides.label: AWS KMS
sides.pickWhen: You want managed keys for AWS encryption integrations.

sides.label: AWS CloudHSM
sides.pickWhen: You need dedicated HSMs under customer control.

difference: EBS is persistent block storage for an instance; EFS and FSx are shared file systems; S3 stores objects in buckets.

sides.label: Amazon EBS
sides.pickWhen: An instance needs persistent low-latency block volumes.

sides.label: Amazon EFS
sides.pickWhen: Linux instances need one shared POSIX file system.

sides.label: Amazon FSx
sides.pickWhen: The workload needs a specific file system, such as Windows or ONTAP.

sides.label: Amazon S3
sides.pickWhen: The data is objects addressed by key.

difference: Aurora Global Database keeps secondary Regions current from the storage layer for disaster recovery and local reads; a cross-Region read replica is a separate replica cluster that serves reads or can be promoted, with engine replication lag.

sides.label: Aurora Global Database
sides.pickWhen: A secondary Region should stay current for disaster recovery and local reads.

sides.label: Cross-Region read replica
sides.pickWhen: Another Region needs its own cluster for queries or a promotable copy.

difference: Site-to-Site VPN is encrypted connectivity over the internet; Direct Connect is a dedicated private circuit.

sides.label: AWS Site-to-Site VPN
sides.pickWhen: You need encrypted connectivity to a VPC without waiting for a dedicated circuit.

difference: Spot uses spare capacity that can be interrupted; Savings Plans discount committed spend across eligible compute; Reserved Instances tie the discount more closely to instance attributes.

sides.pickWhen: The workload can stop and restart, and the discount comes from spare capacity.

sides.label: Reserved Instances
sides.pickWhen: The discount should follow a specific instance family, size, and scope.

difference: A gateway endpoint is a route-table target for S3 or DynamoDB and has no hourly fee; an interface endpoint is a network interface with hourly and data-processing charges.

sides.label: S3 gateway endpoint
sides.pickWhen: Private S3 traffic should leave the NAT path, and the endpoint type should not add an hourly fee.

sides.label: Interface endpoint
sides.pickWhen: The service needs a private address in the subnet, and the hourly and data charges are an acceptable cost.

difference: Standard-IA keeps an infrequently read object in several Availability Zones; One Zone-IA stores it in one zone at a lower price.

sides.label: S3 Standard-IA
sides.pickWhen: Reads are infrequent and immediate, and the object must survive loss of an Availability Zone.

sides.label: S3 One Zone-IA
sides.pickWhen: The object is infrequent, can be recreated, and loss of a single Availability Zone is acceptable.

difference: On-Demand runs without a term commitment and is not taken back for capacity; Spot uses spare capacity and can be interrupted.

sides.label: On-Demand
sides.pickWhen: The work cannot stop, and there is no measured commitment to buy yet.

sides.label: Spot
sides.pickWhen: The work can be interrupted and restarted, and a lower price is worth the capacity risk.

difference: A permissions boundary limits one IAM user or role; a service control policy limits accounts in the organization. Neither statement grants a permission by itself.

sides.label: Permissions boundary
sides.pickWhen: The maximum must be set on one user or role in the account.

sides.label: Service control policy
sides.pickWhen: The guardrail must apply to member accounts in the organization.

difference: A role gives temporary credentials for the session. An IAM user access key is a long-lived secret that has to be stored and rotated.

sides.label: IAM role
sides.pickWhen: The caller should get temporary credentials, and a long-lived key should not sit in the application.

sides.label: IAM user access key
sides.pickWhen: A long-lived key is actually required, and it is not how a person in another account should work.

difference: IAM Identity Center is one workforce sign-in that can reach many accounts. An IAM user created in each account repeats that person once per account.

sides.label: IAM Identity Center
sides.pickWhen: People need one sign-in that can open more than one account.

sides.label: IAM user in each account
sides.pickWhen: The identity should exist only inside one account and does not travel with the person.

difference: A presigned URL is a temporary signature for one private object. A public-read object is readable by anyone who has the URL, with no signature expiry.

sides.label: Presigned URL
sides.pickWhen: One caller needs temporary access and the object must stay private.

sides.label: Public-read object
sides.pickWhen: The object is meant to be readable by anyone. That is the wrong pick when it must stay private.

difference: SSE-KMS uses a KMS key, so a key policy can decide who uses it. SSE-S3 uses a key Amazon S3 manages, and you do not get that key policy.

sides.label: SSE-KMS
sides.pickWhen: You need to decide who can use the key.

sides.label: SSE-S3
sides.pickWhen: S3 should manage the key and a key policy is not required.

difference: Secrets Manager stores a secret and can rotate it. Parameter Store can hold a SecureString, and rotating a database password is the Secrets Manager job.

sides.label: Secrets Manager
sides.pickWhen: A database password should rotate on a schedule.

sides.label: Parameter Store SecureString
sides.pickWhen: The application needs a configuration secret, and password rotation is a separate job.

difference: SQS holds a message until one consumer deletes it. Kinesis Data Streams keeps ordered records in a shard so more than one consumer can read them, including a replay, while they are retained.

sides.label: Amazon SQS
sides.pickWhen: Each message is work for one consumer, and that consumer deletes it when the work is done.

sides.label: Kinesis Data Streams
sides.pickWhen: Several consumers need the same ordered records, and a replay must still be possible.

difference: A FIFO queue adds order within a message group and deduplication, with a lower throughput ceiling. A standard queue offers higher throughput and does not promise that order.

sides.label: SQS FIFO
sides.pickWhen: Messages in one group must be processed in order, and a duplicate should be dropped.

sides.label: SQS standard
sides.pickWhen: Throughput matters more than order, and an occasional duplicate is acceptable.

difference: Failover routing sends traffic from an unhealthy primary record to the secondary. Latency routing sends the user toward the lowest-latency Region and is not a primary-and-secondary failover by itself.

sides.label: Failover routing
sides.pickWhen: Traffic should leave an unhealthy endpoint and use the secondary record.

sides.label: Latency routing
sides.pickWhen: The user should reach the Region with the shortest delay, and you are not naming a primary and a standby.

difference: An EBS snapshot is a point-in-time copy of one volume. AWS Backup is a plan and a vault that can protect many resource types on one schedule.

sides.label: EBS snapshot
sides.pickWhen: You need a point-in-time copy of one volume.

sides.label: AWS Backup
sides.pickWhen: One plan should protect more than one resource type and keep the recovery points in a vault.

difference: A load balancer health check stops sending traffic to a bad target. An Auto Scaling health check can terminate the instance and launch a replacement.

sides.label: Load balancer health check
sides.pickWhen: The bad target should stop receiving requests, and the instance can stay up while it recovers.

sides.label: Auto Scaling health check
sides.pickWhen: The unhealthy instance should be replaced, not only removed from the load balancer.

difference: Lambda runs a function when an event arrives and does not leave a server running. EC2 is an instance that stays up and that you manage.

sides.label: AWS Lambda
sides.pickWhen: The work is a short event-driven function and a server should not stay on between events.

sides.label: Amazon EC2
sides.pickWhen: The process runs for a long time or needs a server you configure and patch.

difference: DynamoDB is a key-value and document database without SQL joins. Aurora is a relational database with a writer that accepts SQL.

sides.label: Amazon DynamoDB
sides.pickWhen: The access is by known keys and the application does not need joins.

sides.label: Amazon Aurora
sides.pickWhen: The data is relational and the application queries it with SQL.

difference: An Application Load Balancer routes HTTP using the path or the host. A Network Load Balancer forwards TCP or UDP and can present a static address.

sides.label: Application Load Balancer
sides.pickWhen: The rule should look at the URL path or the host header.

sides.label: Network Load Balancer
sides.pickWhen: The listeners are TCP or UDP and the clients need a static address.

difference: DMS copies database rows and can keep copying while the source stays online. Glue runs a transform and catalogs the result. It is not that ongoing database replication.

sides.label: AWS DMS
sides.pickWhen: Rows should keep moving to a target database while the source still accepts writes.

sides.label: AWS Glue
sides.pickWhen: A job should transform data and the tables should be listed in the Data Catalog.

difference: S3 Standard is the frequent-access class across several Availability Zones. Standard-IA is for infrequent access that is still immediate, at a lower storage price and with a retrieval charge.

sides.label: S3 Standard
sides.pickWhen: Objects are read often and must come back immediately from more than one Availability Zone.

sides.label: S3 Standard-IA
sides.pickWhen: Reads are infrequent and immediate, and a retrieval charge is an acceptable trade.

difference: A lifecycle rule moves an object on a date you already know. Intelligent-Tiering watches an unknown pattern and moves the object between its own tiers.

sides.label: Lifecycle rule
sides.pickWhen: You already know when the objects become cold.

sides.label: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
sides.pickWhen: The access pattern is unknown and should be monitored instead of guessed.

difference: Aurora Serverless v2 changes capacity with the load, down toward the minimum ACU you set. A provisioned instance stays at the class you selected until you change it.

sides.label: Aurora Serverless v2
sides.pickWhen: The database is idle much of the day and capacity should drop.

sides.label: Provisioned instance
sides.pickWhen: The load is steady and you want a fixed size class.

difference: A NAT gateway charges data processing for traffic that passes through it, including S3 if that is the path. An S3 gateway endpoint is a route-table target with no hourly fee, so that S3 traffic can skip the NAT.

sides.label: NAT gateway
sides.pickWhen: Instances need general outbound internet access, and this S3 traffic is not the part you are taking off the NAT.

sides.label: S3 gateway endpoint
sides.pickWhen: Private subnets should reach S3 without NAT data-processing charges.

difference: Control Tower builds the multi-account setup, the account factory, and the guardrails. Organizations is the account and policy container that sits underneath that setup.

sides.label: AWS Control Tower
sides.pickWhen: The setup still needs guardrails and a factory for new accounts.

sides.label: AWS Organizations
sides.pickWhen: The accounts are already in place, and the work is organization policies.

difference: A user pool is the app's user directory and sign-in. An identity pool trades a trusted identity for temporary AWS credentials.

sides.label: Cognito user pool
sides.pickWhen: The app needs its own sign-in directory and session tokens.

sides.label: Cognito identity pool
sides.pickWhen: A signed-in user needs temporary AWS credentials for a service.

difference: A KMS key policy is the resource policy for that key. Identity-based allows in the same account do nothing until the key policy lets the account use IAM.

sides.label: KMS key policy
sides.pickWhen: The key must name who can use it before other IAM allows apply.

sides.label: IAM identity policy
sides.pickWhen: The key policy already enables IAM, and one role needs an allow.

difference: A cross-account object read needs an allow on the caller and a bucket statement that names that caller. One of those statements still leaves the other account blocked.

sides.label: Bucket policy
sides.pickWhen: The caller role already has its own allow, so the bucket must grant that role.

sides.label: Identity policy
sides.pickWhen: The bucket already grants the role, so the role policy must allow the read.

difference: RAM shares a supported resource, such as a subnet or a resolver rule, into another account. An IAM role lets that account call APIs here.

sides.label: AWS RAM share
sides.pickWhen: Another account should use this subnet or rule inside its own VPC.

sides.label: Cross-account IAM role
sides.pickWhen: The other account should call APIs in this account by assuming an identity you grant.

difference: A NAT gateway is the managed IPv4 egress device for a private subnet. A NAT instance is an EC2 instance you patch, size, and fail over yourself.

sides.label: Managed NAT gateway
sides.pickWhen: Private subnets need an IPv4 path to the internet that AWS operates.

sides.label: NAT instance
sides.pickWhen: The IPv4 egress translator has to be a virtual machine you patch and size.

difference: Client VPN terminates connections from individual users. A site-to-site connection ties a customer gateway on an office network to the VPC.

sides.label: Client VPN
sides.pickWhen: Individual users on laptops need a VPN into the VPC.

sides.label: Site-to-Site VPN
sides.pickWhen: An office network device should have a standing tunnel to the VPC.

difference: WAF applies the HTTP rules you write. Shield is the DDoS protection for the edge. Application-layer match rules still belong in WAF when Shield Advanced is also on.

sides.label: AWS WAF
sides.pickWhen: HTTP requests need match rules for the paths, addresses, or patterns to block.

sides.label: AWS Shield
sides.pickWhen: The workload edge needs protection from a flood of traffic.

difference: GuardDuty watches account, DNS, and flow activity for threats. Inspector scans supported workloads for vulnerable software and reachable ports.

sides.label: Amazon GuardDuty
sides.pickWhen: The team wants alerts on odd API calls, DNS lookups, or flow patterns.

sides.label: Amazon Inspector
sides.pickWhen: The team wants a software and exposure scan of the running workloads.

difference: A security group is the stateful filter on one elastic network interface. Network Firewall sits on the VPC path and can match more than the port.

sides.label: Interface security group
sides.pickWhen: The filter belongs on one machine, by port and source.

sides.label: AWS Network Firewall
sides.pickWhen: The VPC needs a path filter that can look past the port number.

difference: Cognito is the sign-in directory for application customers. IAM users are principals inside the AWS account.

sides.label: Amazon Cognito
sides.pickWhen: Customers of the application need their own sign-in directory.

sides.label: IAM users
sides.pickWhen: The people who need credentials operate this AWS account.

difference: AWS Config records resource configuration and evaluates rules against it. AWS CloudTrail records API activity. A configuration change and the API call that caused it are different records.

sides.label: AWS Config
sides.pickWhen: The record needed is the resource configuration and the rule result.

sides.label: AWS CloudTrail
sides.pickWhen: The record needed is the API caller, the call, and the time.

difference: Browsers already trust a public ACM certificate. A certificate from Private CA is accepted only where that private root is installed.

sides.label: Public ACM certificate
sides.pickWhen: Browsers on the internet must accept the certificate from a well-known trust store.

sides.label: Private CA certificate
sides.pickWhen: Only machines that hold the company root should accept the certificate.

difference: Macie classifies objects in S3 for credentials and personal data. GuardDuty raises threat findings from account and network activity.

sides.label: Amazon Macie
sides.pickWhen: Objects in S3 should be reviewed for credentials or personal data.

sides.label: Amazon GuardDuty
sides.pickWhen: The account should get threat findings from activity, logs, and DNS.

difference: Automatic rotation replaces key material on a period, and the default period is 365 days when you leave it unset. On-demand rotation replaces the material immediately and leaves an existing automatic schedule unchanged. The key id stays put either way, and decrypt uses the material that produced the ciphertext.

sides.label: Automatic key rotation
sides.pickWhen: This symmetric key should get new material on a repeating period.

sides.label: On-demand key rotation
sides.pickWhen: This symmetric key should get new material once, right now.

difference: Viewer HTTPS on CloudFront for a custom domain wants the public certificate in us-east-1 (N. Virginia). A load balancer uses a certificate requested beside the application.

sides.label: Distribution viewer certificate
sides.pickWhen: A custom domain name needs the certificate in us-east-1 (N. Virginia).

sides.label: ACM certificate in the workload Region
sides.pickWhen: The load balancer needs the certificate beside the application.

difference: Amazon SQS is the AWS queue API. Amazon MQ is a managed message broker for applications that already speak AMQP, MQTT, STOMP, OpenWire, or a similar protocol.

sides.label: Amazon SQS queue API
sides.pickWhen: New code can send and receive without speaking a broker protocol.

sides.label: Amazon MQ
sides.pickWhen: Existing code already speaks AMQP, MQTT, or OpenWire.

difference: Amazon SNS fans a message out to subscribers of a topic. Amazon EventBridge routes events by rules on an event bus, including events from AWS services and SaaS partners.

sides.label: Amazon SNS
sides.pickWhen: One published message should reach every subscriber of a topic.

sides.label: Amazon EventBridge
sides.pickWhen: Events should match rules on a bus and go to different targets by content.

difference: Step Functions runs a workflow with state, retries, and branches. SQS holds messages until a worker takes them. A queue does not remember which step of a workflow has finished.

sides.label: AWS Step Functions
sides.pickWhen: The work is a workflow with steps, branches, and a place to resume.

sides.label: Amazon SQS
sides.pickWhen: Each job stands alone, and a worker can take it when the worker is free.

difference: A dead-letter queue receives messages that failed the source queue's receive limit. A Lambda retry retries the invocation. Those are different failure paths.

sides.label: SQS dead-letter queue
sides.pickWhen: A message that exhausts its receive limit should be set aside for inspection.

sides.label: Lambda retry
sides.pickWhen: A failed function invocation should be attempted again by the function service.

difference: EventBridge Scheduler invokes a target on a schedule you define, without an instance that stays running to watch the clock. A cron job on EC2 needs that instance.

sides.label: EventBridge Scheduler
sides.pickWhen: A managed schedule should invoke the target.

sides.label: Cron on an EC2 instance
sides.pickWhen: The schedule should run on a machine you already operate.

difference: A Standard workflow can run for up to a year, runs each state once unless you add a retry, and keeps an execution history. An Express workflow is for short, high-volume runs of at most five minutes, and its guarantee depends on whether that Express workflow is synchronous or asynchronous.

sides.label: Standard workflow
sides.pickWhen: The workflow may run for hours or days, and you need its execution history.

sides.label: Express workflow
sides.pickWhen: The workflow should finish within five minutes and run at high volume.

difference: An S3 event notification sends one bucket's events to a destination you name, such as a queue, topic, or function. EventBridge can receive those events on a bus and route them with rules.

sides.label: S3 event notification
sides.pickWhen: One bucket should send its events straight to a queue, topic, or function.

sides.label: EventBridge for S3 events
sides.pickWhen: Bucket events should land on an event bus and match rules before they reach targets.

difference: Multi-AZ RDS keeps a standby that takes over as the writer. Aurora keeps storage copies across Availability Zones and can add reader endpoints for queries.

sides.label: RDS Multi-AZ standby
sides.pickWhen: One relational database needs a second copy that can take over as the writer.

sides.label: Aurora with readers
sides.pickWhen: Queries should run on extra reader endpoints inside the cluster.

difference: A DynamoDB global table is a multi-Region table that accepts writes in more than one Region. An RDS read replica in another Region is a read copy, and writes still go to the source.

sides.label: DynamoDB global table
sides.pickWhen: Application writes must be accepted in more than one Region.

sides.label: RDS cross-Region read replica
sides.pickWhen: Query traffic should move to another Region, with writes left on the source.

difference: Replication sends newly written objects to a second bucket. AWS Backup stores recovery points on the plan you define for the resources it supports.

sides.label: S3 replication
sides.pickWhen: Newly written objects should show up in a second bucket.

sides.label: AWS Backup plan
sides.pickWhen: Supported resources need recovery points kept on a schedule you define.

difference: Simplified automatic recovery moves that same instance onto healthy hardware after a failed system status check. An Auto Scaling group restores its desired capacity, which can mean a newly launched instance.

sides.label: EC2 automatic recovery
sides.pickWhen: This one instance should restart on new hardware when its system check fails.

sides.label: Auto Scaling replacement
sides.pickWhen: The group should keep its desired count and can launch a new machine.

difference: A failover record changes the address DNS hands out after its health check fails. A load balancer keeps one DNS name and directs new requests toward the healthy targets.

sides.label: Route 53 failover
sides.pickWhen: DNS should hand callers a different endpoint after a health check fails.

sides.label: Load balancer target health
sides.pickWhen: Callers keep one DNS name, and failed targets should get no new requests.

difference: An EBS snapshot is a backup of a volume. An AMI is a template for launching instances, and it can point at snapshots of the volumes that template needs.

sides.label: EBS volume snapshot
sides.pickWhen: One disk needs a point-in-time backup of its blocks.

sides.label: AMI
sides.pickWhen: A new instance should launch from a saved machine image.

difference: Multi-Attach puts one io1 or io2 volume on several Nitro instances that share a zone, and the application has to order the writes. EFS is a file system those instances can mount from different zones.

sides.label: EBS Multi-Attach
sides.pickWhen: Several Nitro instances inside one zone must share the same io2 volume.

sides.label: Amazon EFS
sides.pickWhen: Instances that sit in different zones must mount the same files.

difference: DataSync copies data between on-premises storage and AWS, or between AWS storage services, as a transfer task. Storage Gateway presents cloud storage through a file, volume, or tape interface that stays in the data path.

sides.label: AWS DataSync
sides.pickWhen: The job is a transfer of existing data into AWS or between AWS storage services.

sides.label: AWS Storage Gateway
sides.pickWhen: On-premises applications should keep using a file, volume, or tape interface for cloud storage.

difference: Lustre is the high-throughput file system for compute jobs. The Windows file service speaks SMB and joins Active Directory.

sides.label: FSx for Lustre
sides.pickWhen: Compute jobs need a high-throughput file system for their working data.

sides.label: FSx for Windows File Server
sides.pickWhen: Clients that use SMB need a file system joined to Active Directory.

difference: Lambda runs a function for a single invocation and has a maximum runtime. Fargate runs a container for as long as the task should stay up, without you managing the instances.

sides.label: Lambda for one invocation
sides.pickWhen: The work fits a single short call and then the function ends.

sides.label: AWS Fargate
sides.pickWhen: The work is a container that should stay up for the life of the task.

difference: ECS runs containers from task definitions on AWS's orchestrator. EKS runs the same kind of container from Kubernetes manifests.

sides.label: Amazon ECS
sides.pickWhen: The team will deploy the containers with task definitions.

sides.label: Amazon EKS
sides.pickWhen: The team will deploy the containers with Kubernetes manifests.

difference: A cluster group places the instances near each other inside one Availability Zone. A spread group places the instances on separate hardware.

sides.label: Cluster placement group
sides.pickWhen: These instances should sit close together inside one Availability Zone.

sides.label: Spread placement group
sides.pickWhen: These instances should land on separate racks of hardware.

difference: ElastiCache for Redis supports richer data types, replication, and persistence options. ElastiCache for Memcached is a simple distributed cache with multithreaded nodes and no replication.

sides.label: ElastiCache for Redis
sides.pickWhen: The cache needs replication, richer data types, or persistence options.

sides.label: ElastiCache for Memcached
sides.pickWhen: The cache is a simple key store, and multithreaded nodes matter more than replication.

difference: DAX is a cache in front of DynamoDB that speaks the DynamoDB API. ElastiCache is a separate cache the application reads and writes itself.

sides.label: DynamoDB Accelerator
sides.pickWhen: Table reads should be cached through the same calls the table already uses.

sides.label: Amazon ElastiCache
sides.pickWhen: The application should read and write a cache through the cache's own API.

difference: RDS Proxy sits in front of the database and reuses connections for many brief clients. A larger instance class gives the database itself more CPU, memory, and connection room.

sides.label: RDS Proxy
sides.pickWhen: Many brief clients need a shared pool in front of the database.

sides.label: A larger DB instance
sides.pickWhen: The database itself needs more CPU or memory for its queries.

difference: VPC peering is a connection between two VPCs, and it does not transitive-route through a third VPC. A transit gateway is a hub the VPCs attach to, so many VPCs can share one routing point.

sides.label: VPC peering
sides.pickWhen: Exactly two VPCs need a private path between them.

sides.label: Transit gateway
sides.pickWhen: A larger set of VPCs should share one routing hub.

difference: CloudFront keeps copies of content at edges for viewers. Transfer Acceleration uses the edge network as a faster path for uploads and downloads to one bucket.

sides.label: CloudFront edge cache
sides.pickWhen: Viewers in many places should get a cached copy from a nearby location.

sides.label: S3 Transfer Acceleration
sides.pickWhen: Clients should send and fetch objects through a faster path to one bucket.

services: Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka
difference: Kinesis Data Streams is AWS's own stream, read with the Kinesis API. Amazon MSK is managed Apache Kafka for applications that already produce and consume with Kafka clients.

sides.label: Kinesis Data Streams API
sides.pickWhen: Producers and consumers will call this stream service directly.

sides.label: Amazon MSK
sides.pickWhen: Producers and consumers will keep their Kafka client libraries.

difference: gp3 is general-purpose SSD storage with a baseline you can raise. io2 is provisioned IOPS SSD for sustained high IOPS. Paying for io2 is not required when gp3's IOPS cover the volume.

sides.label: gp3
sides.pickWhen: The volume needs general-purpose SSD performance, and the baseline IOPS are enough.

sides.label: io2
sides.pickWhen: The volume needs sustained provisioned IOPS above what a general-purpose SSD should carry.

difference: EFS Standard is for files you read often. EFS Infrequent Access costs less to store and more to read. Lifecycle policy can move files that have not been read.

sides.label: EFS Standard
sides.pickWhen: These files are read often, and access charges should stay low.

sides.label: EFS Infrequent Access
sides.pickWhen: These files are rarely read, and a lower storage price is worth a higher read price.

difference: Fargate bills for the task's CPU and memory while it runs, and there is no cluster instance to right-size. EC2 container instances can be cheaper when the instances stay full, and you pay for the instances even when tasks do not fill them.

sides.label: AWS Fargate
sides.pickWhen: Tasks come and go, and you do not want to pay for idle container instances.

sides.label: EC2 container instances
sides.pickWhen: The instances stay busy, and paying for those instances is the lower cost.

difference: Budgets sends a notice when cost or usage crosses a threshold you set. Cost Explorer is the place to inspect past spend and a forecast.

sides.label: AWS Budgets
sides.pickWhen: Someone should be notified when cost or usage crosses a threshold.

sides.label: AWS Cost Explorer
sides.pickWhen: Someone needs to inspect past spend or a forecast.

difference: On-demand capacity bills for the requests you make and does not ask for a provisioned rate. Provisioned capacity is a rate you set, and it costs less per request when the traffic is steady enough to use what you bought.

sides.label: On-demand capacity
sides.pickWhen: Traffic is spiky or unknown, and you do not want to set a read and write rate.

sides.label: Provisioned capacity
sides.pickWhen: Traffic is steady enough to buy a read and write rate in advance.

difference: An RDS Reserved Instance discounts a database instance you commit to for a term. On-Demand has no term. The reservation does not change the database engine or the failover design.

sides.label: RDS Reserved Instance
sides.pickWhen: This database will run for the term, and a commitment should lower its hourly price.

sides.label: RDS On-Demand
sides.pickWhen: The database might be stopped or resized before a term would pay off.

difference: A reserved ElastiCache node discounts a node size you commit to. On-demand nodes have no term. The reservation does not add replication or change the engine.

sides.label: Reserved cache node
sides.pickWhen: These cache nodes will run for the term, and the discount should follow that size.

sides.label: On-demand cache node
sides.pickWhen: The cache node size or lifetime is still changing, and a term is too soon.

difference: An interface endpoint puts the AWS API on a private network interface and adds an hourly charge plus data processing. Reaching the public endpoint through a NAT gateway also charges for the NAT data, and the traffic uses the public path.

sides.label: Interface endpoint
sides.pickWhen: This API should stay on a private network address in the subnet, and the hourly charge is acceptable.

sides.label: NAT gateway to the public API
sides.pickWhen: Instances already reach the internet through an egress device, and this API can stay on that path.

difference: A CloudFront price class limits which edge locations can serve the distribution, which can lower the transfer price. Price class All can use every edge. The class does not change the origin.

sides.label: A lower CloudFront price class
sides.pickWhen: Viewers are in the regions a cheaper price class covers, and the transfer price matters.

sides.label: CloudFront price class All
sides.pickWhen: Viewers may be anywhere, and every edge location should stay eligible.

difference: A permission set is a template of IAM policies. Assigning it makes Identity Center create and manage the matching role in each target account. A customer-managed role is one you create and maintain yourself.

sides.label: Identity Center permission set
sides.pickWhen: Workforce access for several accounts should come from a central template that provisions the matching roles.

sides.label: Customer-managed IAM role
sides.pickWhen: Access in a single account should be an identity you create and maintain there yourself.

difference: A service-linked role is predefined and owned by the AWS service, and an administrator can view it but not edit its permissions. A service role is a role an administrator creates, edits, and deletes for a service to assume.

sides.label: Service-linked role
sides.pickWhen: The owning AWS service should receive a predefined role whose permissions that service defines.

sides.label: Service role
sides.pickWhen: An administrator should create, edit, and delete the role a service assumes.

difference: A session policy is passed when a temporary session is created, and that session's permissions are the intersection of the identity-based policies and the session policy. A permissions boundary is a managed policy on the user or role that caps what the identity-based policies can grant.

sides.label: Session policy
sides.pickWhen: The extra ceiling should apply only to the temporary credentials created for this call.

sides.label: Permissions boundary
sides.pickWhen: The ceiling should be attached to the user or role and cap every request that identity makes.

difference: Access Analyzer external access findings identify resources shared with an external entity. Last accessed information shows which services an identity has used so unused access can be removed.

sides.label: IAM Access Analyzer
sides.pickWhen: The team needs findings for resources shared outside the account or the organization.

sides.label: IAM last accessed information
sides.pickWhen: The team needs to see which services an identity has actually used.

difference: An endpoint policy is a resource-based policy on a VPC endpoint that controls which principals can use that endpoint to reach a service. An identity-based policy is attached to the caller. The endpoint policy does not replace the caller's own allow.

sides.label: VPC endpoint policy
sides.pickWhen: The restriction should follow whoever calls through this private entry point.

sides.label: Identity-based policy
sides.pickWhen: The restriction should follow the caller, wherever that caller invokes the service.

difference: Session Manager gives a shell on managed nodes without opening inbound ports, keeping a jump box, or handing out SSH keys. A bastion is an instance people sign in to first.

sides.label: Systems Manager Session Manager
sides.pickWhen: Operators need a shell on private instances, and inbound management ports should stay closed.

sides.label: EC2 bastion host
sides.pickWhen: Operators will sign in to a jump box on a public subnet and then reach the private instances.

difference: Applications on AWS get automatic protection at no additional cost against common volumetric floods such as UDP reflection and SYN floods. Shield Advanced is the managed DDoS service that adds detection, mitigation, and response.

sides.label: AWS Shield Standard
sides.pickWhen: Common volumetric floods, such as UDP reflection and SYN floods, should use the protection already included.

sides.label: AWS Shield Advanced
sides.pickWhen: The application needs the managed DDoS service that adds detection, mitigation, and response.

difference: WAF inspects HTTP and HTTPS requests in front of resources such as CloudFront, API Gateway, and an Application Load Balancer. Network Firewall is a stateful firewall and intrusion prevention service for traffic at the VPC edge and between subnets.

sides.label: AWS Network Firewall
sides.pickWhen: Traffic at the VPC edge, or between subnets, needs inspection beyond web requests.

sides.label: AWS WAF
sides.pickWhen: HTTP requests to a public site should be filtered for patterns such as injection.

difference: GuardDuty is a threat detection service that continuously monitors logs and other AWS data sources. Security Hub CSPM produces its own control findings and also receives findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, and supported partner products.

sides.label: AWS Security Hub
sides.pickWhen: Findings from several detectors should land in one place, next to best-practice checks.

sides.label: GuardDuty threat detection
sides.pickWhen: The account needs continuous analysis of logs for suspicious activity such as odd API calls.

difference: Firewall Manager applies protections such as WAF, Shield Advanced, security groups, network ACLs, and Network Firewall across accounts in an organization, including accounts you add later. A web ACL is the rule set you attach to one protected resource.

sides.label: AWS Firewall Manager
sides.pickWhen: The same protections should be applied across many accounts, including accounts added later.

sides.label: A web ACL on one resource
sides.pickWhen: The HTTP filter should be attached directly to a single public entry.

difference: IMDSv2 is the session-oriented way to read instance metadata. IMDSv1 is the request/response way. An instance can be set to accept only the session-oriented calls.

sides.label: IMDSv2
sides.pickWhen: Metadata reads should use the session-oriented method.

sides.label: IMDSv1
sides.pickWhen: Metadata reads should use the request/response method.

difference: With SSE-C, you send your own encryption key with the request and S3 uses that key as it writes and reads the object. SSE-KMS encrypts with an AWS KMS key, and the key policy should allow only the principals that need that key.

sides.label: SSE-C
sides.pickWhen: The caller should send its own encryption key with each request.

sides.label: SSE-KMS
sides.pickWhen: Objects should be encrypted with a key whose key policy limits the principals.

difference: In compliance mode, no user, including the root user, can overwrite or delete the locked version, and the retention mode cannot be changed or shortened. In governance mode, users with special permission can change the lock or delete the object.

sides.label: S3 Object Lock compliance mode
sides.pickWhen: The lock must hold through the retention date for every user, including the account root.

sides.label: S3 Object Lock governance mode
sides.pickWhen: Most users should be blocked, while a few people with a special permission may change the lock.

difference: Related multi-Region keys share the same key ID and key material in Regions you choose, and each copy works on its own. You create the primary and replicate it. A single-Region key stays in the Region where you created it.

sides.label: Multi-Region KMS key
sides.pickWhen: The same key ID and key material should be available in more than one Region.

sides.label: Single-Region KMS key
sides.pickWhen: The key should stay in the Region where it was created.

difference: Versioning keeps object versions in the bucket. MFA delete is optional on top of versioning: only the bucket owner can turn it on, and removing a version or changing the versioning state then requires two forms of authentication.

sides.label: S3 versioning
sides.pickWhen: Overwrites and removals should leave earlier copies of the object in the bucket.

sides.label: S3 MFA delete
sides.pickWhen: Removing a version, or changing the versioning state, must include a second factor from the bucket owner.

difference: Short polling is a ReceiveMessage call whose wait time is 0, so the call returns without waiting for a message. Long polling lets the call wait and return a message as soon as one is available.

sides.label: SQS long polling
sides.pickWhen: The receive call should wait so a record can be returned as soon as it arrives.

sides.label: SQS short polling
sides.pickWhen: The receive call should use a wait time of zero and come back at once.

difference: While a message is being processed, the visibility timeout keeps it from being retrieved by another consumer. If it is not deleted in time, it becomes visible again. Retention is how long the queue keeps a message that is still there, four days by default and up to 14 days.

sides.label: Visibility timeout
sides.pickWhen: A consumer is working on a received item, and other consumers should leave it alone until that window ends.

sides.label: Message retention period
sides.pickWhen: An unprocessed item should stay in the queue for days before it ages out.

difference: Lambda can send a record of an asynchronous invocation to a destination. Failed attempts, after processing is exhausted, can go to one destination, and successful attempts to another. An SQS dead-letter queue receives a queue message after consumers have received it maxReceiveCount times.

sides.label: Lambda on-failure destination
sides.pickWhen: After async retries are exhausted, the invoke record should be sent to a chosen service.

sides.label: SQS max-receive dead-letter queue
sides.pickWhen: An item should move aside after consumers have taken it too many times.

difference: EventBridge Scheduler creates recurring cron or rate schedules and one-time invocations, with flexible time windows. A scheduled rule runs on a clock as a rule on the event bus, beside that bus's other rules and targets.

sides.label: EventBridge scheduled rule
sides.pickWhen: The schedule should sit with the other rules and targets on the same event bus.

sides.label: EventBridge Scheduler
sides.pickWhen: A one-time call, or a clock run with a flexible window, should be managed centrally.

difference: An SNS subscriber receives every published message unless the subscription has a filter policy. An EventBridge rule uses an event pattern, and matching events are sent to the rule's targets.

sides.label: SNS subscription filter
sides.pickWhen: Each subscriber should receive only the notices that match its own attributes.

sides.label: EventBridge event pattern
sides.pickWhen: A bus should invoke targets only when the incoming record matches a shape you define.

difference: API Gateway creates, publishes, maintains, monitors, and secures REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs. The other entry registers EC2 instances or IP addresses and spreads HTTP requests across them.

sides.label: Amazon API Gateway
sides.pickWhen: Clients need a managed interface for REST or HTTP calls, including publishing and request controls.

sides.label: Application Load Balancer
sides.pickWhen: HTTP requests should be spread across EC2 instances or IP addresses in the VPC.

difference: SQS delivery delay holds a new message before any consumer can receive it. A Step Functions Wait state pauses the state machine until a relative number of seconds passes or an absolute timestamp is reached, then continues.

sides.label: SQS delivery delay
sides.pickWhen: A newly added queue item should stay hidden from consumers for a while.

sides.label: Step Functions Wait state
sides.pickWhen: A workflow should pause until a time you set, then continue.

difference: Pilot light keeps data replication and core infrastructure on in the recovery Region, while application servers are loaded but switched off until a test or a disaster. Warm standby is a scaled-down but fully functional copy that is already running.

sides.label: Pilot light
sides.pickWhen: Core data services stay on in the other Region, and the application servers stay switched off until recovery.

sides.label: Warm standby
sides.pickWhen: A scaled-down but fully functional copy should already be running in the other Region.

difference: In active/active, users can use the workload in any Region where it is deployed. In active/passive, the recovery site starts serving users when a failover event is triggered.

sides.label: Active-active
sides.pickWhen: Users should be able to use the workload in every Region where it is deployed.

sides.label: Active-passive
sides.pickWhen: Users should reach the recovery Region only after a failover event.

difference: One option places object copies in another bucket in this Region. The other places those copies in another Region. Both copy asynchronously, and the buckets may belong to one account or to two.

sides.label: S3 same-Region replication
sides.pickWhen: Object copies should land in another bucket in this Region.

sides.label: S3 cross-Region replication
sides.pickWhen: Object copies should land in a bucket in a different Region.

difference: Geolocation routing sends users to the resource you mapped to their location, such as a continent or a country. Geoproximity routing sends users to the closest resource, and a bias grows or shrinks the area that resource draws from.

sides.label: Geolocation routing
sides.pickWhen: Users in a chosen place, such as a continent, should be sent to the resource you mapped there.

sides.label: Geoproximity routing
sides.pickWhen: Users should reach the closest resource, and a bias can grow or shrink that resource's area.

difference: A Multi-AZ DB instance has one standby that supports failover and does not serve reads. A Multi-AZ DB cluster has standby instances that support failover and can also serve read traffic.

sides.label: Multi-AZ DB instance
sides.pickWhen: Failover capacity should sit aside from reads, with queries staying on the primary.

sides.label: Multi-AZ DB cluster
sides.pickWhen: The extra database copies should accept read queries and also take over if the primary fails.

difference: Weights split traffic across resources by the ratios you set, including while you test a new version. The health-based option keeps users on the primary while that endpoint is healthy and moves them when it is unhealthy.

sides.label: Weighted routing
sides.pickWhen: Several resources should receive traffic at the same time, split by the ratios you set.

sides.label: Failover routing
sides.pickWhen: Traffic should stay on the healthy primary and move when that primary becomes unhealthy.

difference: Instance store is temporary block storage on disks physically attached to the host, suited to buffers, caches, and scratch data. EBS general-purpose SSD volumes are attached volumes for transactional workloads such as databases and interactive apps.

sides.label: Instance store volume
sides.pickWhen: Scratch data, caches, or buffers can use temporary disks physically attached to the host.

sides.label: Amazon EBS volume
sides.pickWhen: A transactional workload needs an attached SSD volume, such as a database disk.

difference: S3 File Gateway presents NFS or SMB, and the files are stored as objects in S3. Volume Gateway presents iSCSI volumes. Cached volumes keep the data in S3 and retain a local copy of frequently used blocks.

sides.label: S3 File Gateway
sides.pickWhen: On-premises clients should use NFS or SMB, with the files stored as objects.

sides.label: Volume Gateway
sides.pickWhen: On-premises servers should use iSCSI, with data in object storage and a local cache of hot blocks.

difference: One option is a physical server fully set aside for you, with visibility, placement control, and host affinity. The other keeps the guest on hardware set aside for this account and isolated from other accounts, without letting you pick the server.

sides.label: EC2 Dedicated Host
sides.pickWhen: The guest should run on a physical server you can place and keep affinity with.

sides.label: EC2 Dedicated Instance
sides.pickWhen: The guest should sit on hardware reserved for this account, without choosing the physical server.

difference: Reserved concurrency sets the maximum and minimum number of concurrent executions for a function, and other functions cannot use that allocation. Provisioned concurrency is the separate control whose logs report initialization duration before the invocation.

sides.label: Reserved concurrency
sides.pickWhen: This function needs a floor and a ceiling on concurrent runs that other functions cannot borrow.

sides.label: Provisioned concurrency
sides.pickWhen: Environments should already be initialized so startup work happens before the request.

difference: DocumentDB is a managed database that runs MongoDB-compatible application code, drivers, and tools. DynamoDB stores items by partition key and retrieves them with that key and any sort key or index.

sides.label: Amazon DocumentDB
sides.pickWhen: The application should keep using MongoDB drivers and the same query tools.

sides.label: Amazon DynamoDB
sides.pickWhen: Items should be stored and fetched by a partition key at any scale.

difference: A global secondary index can use a key schema that differs from the base table, including a different partition key. A local secondary index keeps an alternate sort key for the table's partition key value.

sides.label: DynamoDB global secondary index
sides.pickWhen: Queries need a different partition key than the table uses.

sides.label: DynamoDB local secondary index
sides.pickWhen: Queries use the table's partition key and a different sort key.

difference: A peering connection routes traffic between two VPCs using private IPv4 or IPv6 addresses. PrivateLink connects a VPC privately to a service as if that service were in the VPC.

sides.label: AWS PrivateLink
sides.pickWhen: Consumers should call one service privately, as if that service were inside their own network.

sides.label: VPC peering
sides.pickWhen: Instances in two networks should reach each other by private address.

difference: One option offers addresses that stay the same, advertised from the edge, and improves the path to regional endpoints. The DNS option answers from the Region with the lowest delay to the user.

sides.label: AWS Global Accelerator
sides.pickWhen: Clients should use static anycast addresses and enter over the edge network.

sides.label: Route 53 latency routing
sides.pickWhen: DNS should answer from the Region with the lowest delay between the user and AWS.

difference: Kinesis Video Streams ingests live video from devices. Kinesis Data Streams collects and processes large streams of data records in real time for consumers you build.

sides.label: Kinesis Video Streams
sides.pickWhen: Devices should stream live footage into the cloud for playback or analysis.

sides.label: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
sides.pickWhen: Producers should send records for custom consumers to process in real time.

difference: A crawler connects to a data source, infers the schema, and writes table metadata to the Data Catalog. An ETL job runs the Spark logic that extracts, transforms, and loads the data.

sides.label: AWS Glue crawler
sides.pickWhen: A source should be scanned so its schema lands in the catalog.

sides.label: AWS Glue ETL job
sides.pickWhen: A Spark script should extract, transform, and load records into a target.

difference: EMR is a managed cluster for frameworks such as Hadoop and Spark, and you choose the cluster capacity. Glue is a serverless data integration service for discovering, preparing, and moving data, including running jobs.

sides.label: AWS Glue
sides.pickWhen: The transform should run as a serverless integration for Spark-style processing.

sides.label: Amazon EMR
sides.pickWhen: Hadoop or Spark should run on a cluster the team sizes.

difference: Transfer Family is the managed service for SFTP, AS2, FTPS, FTP, and browser uploads into and out of AWS storage, and existing clients can keep their authentication. DataSync moves file or object data at high speed to, from, and between AWS storage, including from NFS, SMB, and HDFS.

sides.label: AWS Transfer Family
sides.pickWhen: Partners should keep using SFTP, FTPS, FTP, or AS2 clients and land files in AWS storage.

sides.label: AWS DataSync
sides.pickWhen: Large file sets should move at high speed from NFS, SMB, or HDFS, or between AWS storage services.

difference: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval restores in minutes to 12 hours. S3 Glacier Deep Archive restores in 9 to 48 hours. You pick the class by how often you read the data and how fast the restore must finish.

sides.label: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
sides.pickWhen: A restore that finishes in minutes, or within 12 hours, fits this archive.

sides.label: S3 Glacier Deep Archive
sides.pickWhen: A restore window of 9 to 48 hours fits this colder archive.

difference: gp2 volumes burst above baseline by spending I/O credits, up to 3,000 IOPS for smaller volumes. gp3 volumes cost 20 percent less per GiB than gp2 and are designed to deliver their provisioned performance.

sides.label: gp2 volume
sides.pickWhen: The general-purpose SSD should burst above its baseline by spending I/O credits.

sides.label: gp3 volume
sides.pickWhen: The general-purpose SSD should cost less per GiB and deliver the performance you provision.

difference: The flexible compute commitment follows usage across families, sizes, Regions, operating systems, and tenancy, and it also follows Fargate and Lambda. The page compares that price with the uncommitted rate.

sides.label: Compute Savings Plan
sides.pickWhen: Steady usage can shift across instance families, Regions, Fargate, or Lambda, and a spend commitment is acceptable.

sides.label: On-Demand compute
sides.pickWhen: Usage should be billed at the uncommitted price and can stop when the work stops.

difference: A Standard Reserved Instance has the larger discount, and you cannot exchange it. A Convertible Reserved Instance can be exchanged, with a smaller discount.

sides.label: Standard Reserved Instance
sides.pickWhen: The larger discount fits, and this reservation stays as purchased.

sides.label: Convertible Reserved Instance
sides.pickWhen: The reservation should be exchangeable for a different configuration later.

difference: One entry places firewall and intrusion-detection appliances in the path and scales those appliances. The other entry spreads TCP, UDP, and TLS flows across registered targets.

sides.label: Network Load Balancer
sides.pickWhen: TCP or UDP clients need a stable entry that spreads load across the targets.

sides.label: Gateway Load Balancer
sides.pickWhen: Traffic should pass through virtual firewall or inspection appliances that scale with demand.

difference: Reserved capacity is a commitment to a minimum amount of provisioned throughput on Standard-class tables. On-demand mode is pay-per-request, and you do not set a read or write throughput figure ahead of time.

sides.label: DynamoDB reserved capacity
sides.pickWhen: Provisioned throughput on the Standard table class should be covered by a commitment to a minimum amount.

sides.label: DynamoDB on-demand mode
sides.pickWhen: Reads and writes should be pay-per-request, and nobody sets a throughput figure in advance.

difference: Database Savings Plans cover AWS database services and can reduce Aurora and RDS cost, while still letting you use those database services. Paying as you go has no term commitment.

sides.label: Database Savings Plan
sides.pickWhen: A commitment should cover Aurora and RDS, and the database choice can still change.

sides.label: Uncommitted database price
sides.pickWhen: The bill should follow actual database use, and there is no term commitment.

difference: Transfer Acceleration sends uploads to a CloudFront edge location and then to S3 over an optimized path. Additional data transfer charges can apply. Clients close to the bucket's Region can send objects to that Region directly.

sides.label: S3 Transfer Acceleration
sides.pickWhen: Distant clients should send objects through an edge location, and the added charge is acceptable.

sides.label: Regional S3 upload
sides.pickWhen: Clients close to the bucket's Region should send objects straight to that Region.

difference: A NAT gateway lets private-subnet instances open outbound connections. Unsolicited inbound connections stay blocked. Cost-conscious designs compare one shared egress device with a separate egress device in every zone.

sides.label: Shared NAT gateway
sides.pickWhen: Private subnets can send outbound traffic through the same device, which keeps the egress footprint small.

sides.label: NAT gateway per Availability Zone
sides.pickWhen: Private subnets in separate locations keep an outbound path of their own, so one location's loss leaves the others connected.

difference: For the same prefix, a virtual private gateway prefers BGP routes from Direct Connect over Site-to-Site VPN routes. The VPN path is the lower-priority route. Stopping at the dedicated circuit leaves no second path when that route is gone.

sides.label: Direct Connect only
sides.pickWhen: One private circuit covers the volume, so a second connection is extra cost to run.

sides.label: Direct Connect plus VPN backup
sides.pickWhen: The private circuit stays preferred, and an encrypted internet path takes over if that circuit is down.

difference: HDD volumes are for large streaming transfers, where throughput is the limit. General Purpose SSD volumes are for transactional work made of small reads and writes, where IOPS is the limit.

sides.label: Throughput Optimized HDD
sides.pickWhen: Large sequential transfers should stay on the magnetic volume built for that access pattern.

sides.label: General Purpose SSD
sides.pickWhen: Small random reads and writes need the solid-state volume with steady IOPS.

difference: Elastic throughput scales with the workload, and you pay for the data read or written. Provisioned throughput is a transfer rate you set, and you are charged for the amount you enable.

sides.label: EFS elastic throughput
sides.pickWhen: The file system should raise and lower its transfer rate with a spiky load.

sides.label: EFS provisioned throughput
sides.pickWhen: The file system needs a transfer rate you set ahead of the load.

difference: Fast Snapshot Restore makes volumes created from a snapshot deliver full performance immediately. Without it, the volume fills blocks as they are first read.

sides.label: Fast Snapshot Restore
sides.pickWhen: Volumes created from this copy must run at full speed on the first read.

sides.label: A plain EBS snapshot
sides.pickWhen: The first reads can fill in slowly, which is enough for a backup copy.

difference: Express One Zone stores data inside a single Availability Zone and targets the lowest object latency. The Standard class is built to survive loss of a location in the Region.

sides.label: S3 Express One Zone
sides.pickWhen: Objects stay in a single location and the application needs the lowest object latency.

sides.label: S3 Standard storage
sides.pickWhen: Objects must remain available if a location in the Region is lost.

difference: Multipart upload sends a large object as pieces, and a failed piece can be sent again. A single operation sends the whole object in one request.

sides.label: S3 multipart upload
sides.pickWhen: A large object should go up in pieces that can retry on their own.

sides.label: S3 single-part upload
sides.pickWhen: The object is small enough to send in one request.

difference: Cached volumes keep a working set on the appliance and store the volume data in Amazon S3. Stored volumes keep the dataset on the appliance and back it up to Amazon S3 asynchronously.

sides.label: Cached volume gateway
sides.pickWhen: Recent files stay on the appliance, and the full copy lives in S3.

sides.label: Stored volume gateway
sides.pickWhen: The whole dataset stays on the appliance, with async copies sent to S3.

difference: Partition placement spreads members so they avoid sharing a rack. Cluster placement packs members together to cut latency between them.

sides.label: Partition placement group
sides.pickWhen: Instances should be split across racks so a rack failure leaves other groups running.

sides.label: Cluster placement in a rack
sides.pickWhen: Instances should sit close together for the lowest latency between them.

difference: Target tracking holds a metric near a chosen value by changing capacity. Step scaling applies the increments you define when a metric crosses a bound.

sides.label: Target tracking scaling
sides.pickWhen: Capacity should follow a metric toward a number you choose.

sides.label: Step scaling policy
sides.pickWhen: Capacity should jump by an amount you set when a metric crosses a bound.

difference: An ELB check removes a member the load balancer marks unhealthy. An EC2 check removes a member whose status check has failed.

sides.label: ELB health for the group
sides.pickWhen: Replace a member when the traffic distribution marks it failed.

sides.label: Instance status for the group
sides.pickWhen: Replace a member when the hypervisor reports the machine has failed.

difference: Predictive scaling uses past load to add capacity before a repeating pattern. Target tracking changes capacity after the metric leaves the value you set.

sides.label: Predictive scaling policy
sides.pickWhen: Add capacity before a repeating daily pattern arrives.

sides.label: Reactive tracking policy
sides.pickWhen: Change size after the metric has already moved away from the goal.

difference: A warm pool keeps initialized instances stopped so a scale-out can start them. Without a warm pool, the group launches instances when demand grows.

sides.label: ASG warm pool
sides.pickWhen: Stopped copies should be ready so a scale-out skips a full boot.

sides.label: ASG cold launch
sides.pickWhen: New machines should boot only when the group actually grows.

difference: Lambda assigns CPU in proportion to the function memory setting. Reserved concurrency is a cap on how many copies of the function run at once.

sides.label: Higher function memory
sides.pickWhen: A single invocation needs extra CPU, and the size setting is what raises CPU.

sides.label: A higher concurrency cap
sides.pickWhen: Many copies must be allowed to run at the same time, up to a limit you choose.

difference: The reader endpoint spreads connections across Aurora replicas. The writer endpoint sends connections to the primary instance.

sides.label: Aurora reader endpoint
sides.pickWhen: Queries should land on the copies that serve reads.

sides.label: Aurora writer endpoint
sides.pickWhen: Inserts and updates must land on the primary.

difference: MemoryDB keeps a durable transaction log so writes survive a restart. ElastiCache is a cache that can be rebuilt from the database.

sides.label: Amazon MemoryDB
sides.pickWhen: The in-memory store must keep a durable log so writes survive a restart.

sides.label: ElastiCache as a cache
sides.pickWhen: A temporary copy can be rebuilt from the database after it is emptied.

difference: A read replica can serve queries and may lag behind the writer. A Multi-AZ standby is there to take over as the writer and is not a general query target.

sides.label: RDS read replica
sides.pickWhen: Extra copies should serve queries and can lag behind the writer.

sides.label: RDS standby copy
sides.pickWhen: A second machine should take over as the writer when the first fails.

difference: Storage autoscaling grows the allocated disk after free space falls, and it stops at a maximum you set. A fixed allocation stays at the size chosen at creation.

sides.label: RDS storage autoscaling
sides.pickWhen: Allocated disk should grow when free space gets low, up to a ceiling.

sides.label: A fixed storage allocation
sides.pickWhen: Allocated disk should stay at the amount chosen when it was created.

difference: Cluster mode enabled partitions the data across as many as 500 shards. Cluster mode disabled always keeps one shard, and that shard can include read replicas.

sides.label: Redis cluster mode
sides.pickWhen: The dataset should be partitioned so it can grow across many shards.

sides.label: Single-shard Redis
sides.pickWhen: The dataset fits in one primary group, and partitioning it is extra moving parts.

difference: A strongly consistent read returns the latest successful write. An eventually consistent read may return a slightly earlier value and consumes fewer read capacity units.

sides.label: Strongly consistent read
sides.pickWhen: The call must return the latest successful write.

sides.label: Eventually consistent read
sides.pickWhen: The call can return a slightly stale copy and uses less read capacity.

difference: CloudFront Functions run short JavaScript for viewer-request changes. Lambda@Edge runs a Lambda function at the edge when the code needs a broader runtime or network access.

sides.label: CloudFront Functions
sides.pickWhen: A short viewer-request change should run close to the viewer.

sides.label: Lambda at the edge
sides.pickWhen: The code near the viewer needs a fuller runtime or network calls.

difference: An alias record can point at selected AWS resources, including the zone apex. A CNAME points at another hostname and cannot be placed at the zone apex.

sides.label: Route 53 alias record
sides.pickWhen: The name should point at an AWS resource, including the apex of the zone.

sides.label: Route 53 CNAME record
sides.pickWhen: The name should point at another hostname outside the apex of the zone.

difference: An edge-optimized endpoint sends callers to a nearby CloudFront point of presence, which helps when clients are spread across geographies. A Regional endpoint is for clients in the same Region and reduces connection overhead there.

sides.label: Edge-optimized API endpoint
sides.pickWhen: Callers are spread across many places, so requests should enter at a nearby point of presence.

sides.label: Regional API endpoint
sides.pickWhen: Callers are in the same Region as the API, so a nearer point of presence is unused.

difference: Geolocation routing chooses a record from the caller's location. Weighted routing sends a proportion of queries to each record at the same time.

sides.label: Geolocation by caller
sides.pickWhen: The DNS answer should depend on where the person is.

sides.label: Weighted share of queries
sides.pickWhen: The DNS answer should send a chosen fraction of lookups to each target.

difference: HTTP APIs are aimed at lower latency and a smaller feature set. REST APIs add API keys, usage plans, and request validation.

sides.label: API Gateway HTTP API
sides.pickWhen: The front door needs lower latency and a smaller feature set.

sides.label: API Gateway REST API
sides.pickWhen: The front door needs usage plans, API keys, or request validation.

difference: A private hosted zone resolves names inside the VPCs you associate. A public hosted zone resolves names on the internet.

sides.label: Private hosted zone
sides.pickWhen: Names should resolve only inside the VPCs you associate.

sides.label: Public hosted zone
sides.pickWhen: Names should resolve for callers on the internet.

difference: SQS hands a message to a consumer, and the consumer deletes it after the work succeeds. Kinesis Data Streams keeps records so more than one consumer can read them and read them again.

sides.label: SQS work queue
sides.pickWhen: Each job should be taken by one consumer and removed after success.

sides.label: Kinesis replay stream
sides.pickWhen: Several consumers should read the same records and move back over them.

difference: Athena runs SQL over data in S3 and does not require a cluster you manage. Redshift is a data warehouse you size for repeated analytical queries.

sides.label: Amazon Athena
sides.pickWhen: SQL should run over files in S3 without a cluster you operate.

sides.label: Amazon Redshift
sides.pickWhen: SQL should run on a warehouse you size for frequent queries.

difference: Glue DataBrew prepares data with visual steps. A Glue ETL job runs a script you provide.

sides.label: Glue DataBrew
sides.pickWhen: Analysts should clean data with visual steps on a console.

sides.label: Glue code job
sides.pickWhen: The transform should be a script that runs on a schedule you control.

difference: A provisioned MSK cluster is brokers you choose and size. MSK Serverless scales capacity without broker sizing.

sides.label: MSK provisioned cluster
sides.pickWhen: You choose how many brokers to run and how large each one is.

sides.label: MSK serverless cluster
sides.pickWhen: Capacity should grow and shrink without broker sizing.

difference: AppFlow moves records between SaaS applications and AWS. DataSync copies file-system data to and from AWS storage.

sides.label: Amazon AppFlow
sides.pickWhen: SaaS applications should send records into AWS on a schedule or an event.

sides.label: DataSync file movement
sides.pickWhen: Network storage should copy datasets into S3 or another storage system.

difference: Lake Formation grants access to databases, tables, and columns in the catalog. A bucket policy allows or denies S3 actions on the bucket.

sides.label: Lake Formation grants
sides.pickWhen: Table-level permissions should control who can query the catalog.

sides.label: Bucket policy only
sides.pickWhen: Access should stay on the object store's own rules.

difference: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval returns rarely accessed archive objects in milliseconds. S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval is for archives you restore, with retrieval times from minutes to hours.

sides.label: Glacier Instant Retrieval
sides.pickWhen: Rarely read archive objects must still return in milliseconds.

sides.label: Glacier Flexible Retrieval
sides.pickWhen: Archive objects can wait minutes or hours while a restore runs.

difference: Cold HDD is for sequential data that is accessed infrequently, where the lowest storage cost matters. Throughput Optimized HDD is for sequential data that is accessed often, with a higher throughput ceiling.

sides.label: Cold HDD volume
sides.pickWhen: Sequential data is scanned rarely, so the lowest storage cost matters.

sides.label: Busy sequential HDD
sides.pickWhen: Sequential data is scanned often and needs the higher throughput ceiling.

difference: Unfinished multipart parts keep incurring storage charges until the upload is completed or stopped. A lifecycle rule can abort those uploads after a number of days.

sides.label: Lifecycle abort of partial uploads
sides.pickWhen: A rule should delete unfinished pieces after a set number of days.

sides.label: Manual stop of partial uploads
sides.pickWhen: The application should finish or cancel each upload itself.

difference: The archive tier is for snapshots you will store 90 days or longer and rarely restore, at up to 75 percent lower storage cost. The standard tier keeps incremental snapshots ready to use.

sides.label: Snapshot archive tier
sides.pickWhen: A copy you rarely restore can move to the long-term tier.

sides.label: Snapshot standard tier
sides.pickWhen: A copy you may restore soon should stay ready to use.

difference: Intelligent-Tiering moves objects as access changes and charges a monitoring fee, with no retrieval fee. Standard-IA charges a retrieval fee and fits infrequent access you already expect.

sides.label: Intelligent-Tiering for shifting access
sides.pickWhen: The pattern changes, so objects should move when they go quiet.

sides.label: Standard-IA for predictable rare reads
sides.pickWhen: Retrievals follow an infrequent pattern, and a fee on each retrieval is acceptable.

difference: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan discounts a chosen instance family in one Region. A Compute Savings Plan follows usage across families, sizes, Regions, and also covers Fargate and Lambda.

sides.label: EC2 Instance Savings Plan
sides.pickWhen: The discount should stay on a chosen family in one Region.

sides.label: Compute Savings Plan span
sides.pickWhen: The discount should follow usage across families, sizes, and services.

difference: T instances earn CPU credits below a baseline and spend them when they burst. M instances provide CPU without a credit balance.

sides.label: Burstable T family
sides.pickWhen: CPU is quiet most of the time and can draw a balance of credits.

sides.label: Steady M family
sides.pickWhen: CPU stays busy and needs a constant share of the processor.

difference: Hibernation writes RAM to the root volume so the instance resumes its processes. Stopping the instance drops RAM, and the next start boots again.

sides.label: EC2 hibernation
sides.pickWhen: The memory contents should be saved so the process resumes after the pause.

sides.label: EC2 stop then start
sides.pickWhen: The machine can boot fresh after the pause, with memory starting empty.

difference: A scheduled action changes group capacity at times you set. Holding peak capacity keeps the busy-hour size in place all day.

sides.label: Scheduled scaling action
sides.pickWhen: Busy hours are known, so the group should grow and shrink on the clock.

sides.label: Peak capacity held all day
sides.pickWhen: The group should stay at the busy-hour size through the whole period.

difference: A Dedicated Host gives you visibility of the physical server so socket-based licenses can be bound to it. Shared tenancy places instances on hardware that other customers also use.

sides.label: Dedicated Host for licenses
sides.pickWhen: Per-socket software should bind to a physical server you can see.

sides.label: Shared tenancy hardware
sides.pickWhen: The software can run on multi-tenant machines with other customers.

difference: Aurora I/O-Optimized has higher instance and storage rates and no charge for read or write I/O. It can cost less when I/O is 25 percent or more of Aurora spend. Aurora Standard charges per million I/O requests and is typically the lower bill when I/O is under 25 percent.

sides.label: Aurora I/O-Optimized
sides.pickWhen: I/O is a large share of the bill, so a higher storage rate with I/O included fits.

sides.label: Aurora Standard config
sides.pickWhen: I/O is a modest share of the bill, so a per-million request charge fits.

difference: DynamoDB Standard-IA is for tables where storage is the dominant cost, such as infrequently read data. DynamoDB Standard is priced for tables whose requests are a larger share of the bill. Each class prices storage and requests differently.

sides.label: DynamoDB Standard-IA table
sides.pickWhen: The table holds data that is rarely read, and storage is the dominant cost.

sides.label: DynamoDB Standard table
sides.pickWhen: The table is read and written often enough that storage is a smaller share of the bill.

difference: TTL removes an item after the expiry timestamp stored on that item. Without TTL, items remain until the application deletes them.

sides.label: DynamoDB TTL expiry
sides.pickWhen: Rows should disappear after a timestamp stored on them.

sides.label: Items kept until deleted
sides.pickWhen: Rows should remain for as long as the application chooses to remove them.

difference: Automated backups allow point-in-time restore within the retention window. Manual snapshots are copies you take and keep until you delete them.

sides.label: Automated RDS backups
sides.pickWhen: Point-in-time restore inside a retention window should be available.

sides.label: Operator-taken RDS copies
sides.pickWhen: The snapshots a person takes should be the ones that are kept.

difference: An Aurora reader is another database instance in the cluster that serves queries. A cache serves repeated results from memory so the database receives fewer of those calls.

sides.label: Aurora reader for queries
sides.pickWhen: Read volume should be served by another copy in the cluster.

sides.label: Memory cache in front of Aurora
sides.pickWhen: Repeated results should be served from a fast store so the database sees fewer calls.

difference: A NAT instance is an EC2 instance you patch and size, billed as that instance. A NAT gateway is managed by AWS and billed by how many you run, how long they run, and the data you send through them.

sides.label: Self-managed NAT machine
sides.pickWhen: Low volume can run on a computer you patch and size yourself.

sides.label: Managed NAT service
sides.pickWhen: Outbound traffic should use a managed path billed by time and by data processed.

difference: Creating a VPC peering connection has no charge, and it joins two VPCs. It does not forward traffic onward to a third VPC. A transit gateway is the hub when many VPCs must reach one another.

sides.label: Peering between two VPCs
sides.pickWhen: A pair of networks should connect directly, and creating that link has no charge.

sides.label: A transit hub for VPCs
sides.pickWhen: A group of networks should each attach once to a central router.

difference: Data transfer inside the same Availability Zone is free. Data transfer between Availability Zones in the Region is charged.

sides.label: Same-AZ data path
sides.pickWhen: The hop stays inside one location, so that transfer is free.

sides.label: Cross-AZ data path
sides.pickWhen: The hop crosses locations in the Region, and that transfer is billed.

difference: CloudFront can serve a cached copy to later viewers. A direct read from the bucket goes to S3 for every request.

sides.label: CloudFront for repeated gets
sides.pickWhen: The same objects are fetched by many viewers, so an edge copy should absorb the repeats.

sides.label: Direct bucket gets
sides.pickWhen: Each object is fetched once, so viewers can read the origin straight.

difference: Public IPv4 addresses are billed. An instance with only private addresses reaches the internet through NAT, which has its own charges, and does not hold a public address of its own.

sides.label: Public IPv4 on the instance
sides.pickWhen: Callers outside the VPC must reach the machine on a number of its own.

sides.label: Private addressing only
sides.pickWhen: The machine should stay off the internet and reach outbound through NAT.
